intro: This capstone puts the whole course to work in two ways. First, you become the scientist. With a tape measure, a phone camera, a bubble level and a luggage scale, you measure your own speed, the slope of a path, the friction on a waxed and an unwaxed ledge, the hang time of an ollie and the energy you keep on a ramp. Each test uses the physics from earlier units: speed as distance over time, friction as μ times weight, h = g × t² ÷ 8 for a jump and v = √(2gh) for a drop.

Second, you become an advocate. Most public skateparks exist because a group of ordinary people asked for one, counted who would use it, answered their neighbors' worries and stood up at a city council meeting. You will follow that path from a first sketch to a written proposal, using history from Burnside, the Southbank undercroft and Skateistan, and design ideas that make room for beginners, girls and women, and wheelchair riders.

By the end you will be able to run a simple experiment safely, show every step of the arithmetic, report a result with its uncertainty, and write a proposal that backs each claim with evidence. The two halves meet in the middle: the slope you measure and the sound level you record become facts a council can trust.
bigQuestion: How can careful measurement and steady community work turn skating into knowledge, and a wish into a public place?

timeline.t: Isaac Newton publishes the Principia, setting out the laws of motion used to predict speed and force
First National Skateboard Championships held in Anaheim, California
Carlsbad Skatepark in California and Skateboard City in Florida open
Many paid skateparks close over the cost of insurance
Skaters begin building Burnside under a bridge in Portland, Oregon
The Tony Hawk Foundation is founded to help towns build public skateparks
Oliver Percovich founds Skateistan in Kabul, Afghanistan
An agreement keeps the Southbank undercroft in London open for skating
The International Olympic Committee adds skateboarding to the Games
The Tony Hawk Foundation is renamed The Skatepark Project
Skateboarding makes its Olympic debut at Tokyo 2020, held a year late

words.d: the total distance traveled divided by the total time taken
how many still pictures a video records each second
the steepness of a slope, often written as a percent: rise ÷ run × 100
μ, the friction force divided by the force pressing two surfaces together
the time a board or rider spends in the air between take-off and landing
the range a measurement could reasonably be off by, given the tools used
energy stored by height, equal to mass × g × height (mgh)
a testable guess about what will happen, with a reason
people who speak up and work for a cause, such as a new skatepark
money set aside in a budget for problems or costs no one expected
a park that mixes street features and transition in one design
easy to reach and use for people of all abilities, including wheelchair users

test.q: A rider covers a 10.0 m gate in 2.0 s. What is the average speed?
A clip at 30 frames per second shows a run of 120 frames. How long was the run?
What does filming from far back and square to the gate reduce?
test.why: A distant camera square to the path views each mark nearly straight on, which shrinks parallax.

test.q: A 1.00 m level board has its low end lifted 0.04 m. What is the grade?
A 49 N load slides with a steady 12.25 N pull. What is μ?
Why is the tug at the start of a slide larger than the steady pull?
choices: Static friction is usually larger than kinetic friction
The scale reads double at first
test.why: Surfaces at rest grip harder than surfaces already sliding.

test.q: An ollie has a hang time of 0.40 s. Using h = g × t² ÷ 8, about how high did the board rise?
A drop from 1.2 m predicts 4.85 m/s, but the video shows 4.3 m/s. What explains the gap?
choices: The formula is wrong for ramps
Energy went to friction, air, sound and the rider's legs
test.why: The formula ignores losses, and real rides lose energy along the way.

test.q: Which part of a lab report lists every step so someone else could repeat the test?
test.why: The method records the steps, tools and conditions of the test.

test.q: Why did many paid skateparks of the late 1970s close in the early 1980s?
test.why: Insurance became too expensive for many paid parks.

test.q: What is the role of a city council in building a public skatepark?
choices: It approves the plans and the money
test.why: The council controls the budget, so it makes the final decision.

test.q: Which skatepark area is built like a city square with ledges, rails and banks?
test.why: A street plaza copies city features in a legal space.

test.q: In open air, sound measures 80 dB at 10 m. About what is it at 20 m?
test.why: Doubling the distance lowers the level by about 6 dB: 80 − 6 = 74 dB.

test.q: Which skater-built park began under a bridge in Portland, Oregon, in 1990?
test.why: Skaters began building Burnside under the Burnside Bridge in 1990.

test.q: Which design choice best serves beginners?
choices: Placing the beginner area where fast lines cross
A separate area with low banks and clear sightlines
test.why: A beginner area to one side, with small features and clear views, keeps learners safe.

write.prompt: Pick one experiment from this unit, such as the hang-time test or the waxed ledge, and explain it as a worked example: the question, the method, the numbers with every step of the arithmetic, and what the result means. Then explain how that kind of measurement could support a skatepark proposal.
tips: Write each formula before you put numbers into it.
Show units at every step, such as m, s, N or m/s.
Give your result with its uncertainty or range.
Name one source of error and how you would reduce it.
Connect the number to a decision a council or a skater could make.
